title: Saturday at Six. Why the Market Feeds More Than the Week
body: The market opens at six and is basically finished by ten, and the difference between the market and the supermarket is not the vegetables. The vegetables overlap almost completely. The difference is that the market is a conversation that has been running, without interruption, for decades, and I only found out because I started going at six instead of nine. At nine you shop. At six you arrive. The difference is the difference between walking into a party at the end and being there when the table is set. The crates come off the trucks still cold. The first customers are not shoppers, they are the other stall owners buying their own lunch from each other, and the banter between them is the market's real clock. My anchor is the herb stall at the north entrance, run by a man who sells parsley in amounts calibrated to actual households. Not a bunch the size of a small tree. A bunch for a real week. He asks what you are cooking before he chooses the bunch, and he has never once been wrong about the amount. I asked him how long he has been there. He said, without looking up, that his father had this spot, and his grandfather had a spot near it, and the market itself moved twice, and the spot is the only address he has ever trusted. The social physics of the market run on small repeated contact. The cheese woman knows my mother's order. The egg man saves the double yolk cartons for a customer I have never identified, and we have all agreed not to ask. A new stall tried to open with printed price signs and laminated displays, and the market absorbed it politely the way a body absorbs a splinter, and within a season the signs were gone and the owner was shouting prices by hand like everyone else. The market has a dress code that is never written and never violated. What the week gets from all this is not just better vegetables, though the tomatoes are a scandal that supermarkets should answer for. The week gets a fabric. On Tuesday, when my neighbor needed someone to receive a delivery, the ask took ten seconds, because we had already exchanged forty small good mornings at the market. Trust at that speed is not built by conversation. It is built by co-presence, repeated, at the same hour, in the same place, over years. Institutions pay consultants to invent what the market does automatically. The economics deserve honesty too. Some stall prices are higher than the large stores. Some are lower, dramatically, at the end of the morning. The value is not uniformly cheap. The value is legible. I can see the cucumbers, ask who grew them, get told, and believe it or not believe it, and choose. In the supermarket, the cucumber is a stranger with a barcode. Here the cucumber has a cousin who goes to my gym. Six is early. The alarm is rude and the coffee at home is rushed. But by six forty I am walking home with herbs calibrated to my actual cooking, bread still warm, and the specific full feeling of having been somewhere where people know what I buy. The fridge is not the only thing that gets stocked on Saturday. Something quieter gets stocked too, and it lasts all week.
